keyTakeaways: The Republic's October bank holiday is the last Monday of the month: 26 October 2026 and 25 October 2027; Northern Ireland has none.
Department of Education Circular 0018/2026 closes all schools 26–30 October 2026 and 25–29 October 2027, giving nine days off with Halloween on the closing weekend.
A 1930s Blarney record lists five barmbrack charms: a ring (marriage within twelve months), a pea, a bean, a stick and a rag.

faqs.question: Is Halloween a public holiday in Ireland?
faqs.answer: Not 31 October itself. The Republic's public holiday is the last Monday in October, set by the Organisation of Working Time Act 1997, which is Monday 26 October 2026 and Monday 25 October 2027. Northern Ireland has no October bank holiday.

faqs.question: When do Irish schools close for the Halloween mid-term break?
faqs.answer: Department of Education Circular 0018/2026 closes all schools from Monday 26 to Friday 30 October 2026 and from Monday 25 to Friday 29 October 2027. With the weekends either side, that is nine days off in a row both years.

faqs.question: What do people eat on Halloween in Ireland?
faqs.answer: Barmbrack is the food most tied to the night. Nic Philibín's 2025 study of the 1937 to 1939 Schools' Collection also names colcannon, boxty and apple cake among the dishes children listed for the feast.

faqs.question: What charms go inside a barmbrack?
faqs.answer: A 1930s pupil in Blarney, Co. Cork listed a ring, a pea, a bean, a stick and a rag. Whoever got the ring was said to marry within twelve months; the record does not explain the other four, so treat any modern list of meanings with care.

faqs.question: Are Halloween bonfires legal in Ireland?
faqs.answer: No. Dublin Fire Brigade's Halloween page says bonfires are illegal and asks people to attend organised events only. It receives hundreds of 999 and 112 calls about bonfires over Halloween, especially on the 31st.

faqs.question: Can I set off fireworks in Ireland on Halloween night?
faqs.answer: Igniting a firework is an offence under section 80 of the Explosives Act 1875 as rewritten by the Criminal Justice Act 2006, with a maximum of a €10,000 fine or five years in prison on indictment. Low-hazard fireworks other than bangers fall outside that offence; this is a summary, not legal advice.

faqs.question: How do you say Halloween in Irish?
faqs.answer: Oíche Shamhna. The Ó Dónaill dictionary glosses it as Hallowe'en, gives Lá Samhna as the first of November, and shows that Samhain is also the Irish word for November.

faqs.question: Is Derry Halloween in Ireland or the UK?
faqs.answer: Both, in a sense: Derry is on the island of Ireland but in Northern Ireland, which is part of the UK. Its festival runs 28 October to 1 November 2026, with the parade and fireworks on 31 October, and you pay in sterling.

faqs.question: What is the Púca, and when is the Púca Festival?
faqs.answer: A púca is a hobgoblin or pooka in Irish folklore. The festival named after it runs 29 October to 1 November 2026 in Trim and Athboy, Co. Meath; 2027 dates had not been announced in October 2026, so check the official site.

faqs.question: Did Irish people carve turnips instead of pumpkins?
faqs.answer: Turnip lanterns are on record: a 1930s Schools' Collection entry from Bunninadden, Co. Sligo describes a carved turnip with a candle. The popular claim that the jack-o'-lantern is an ancient Irish invention is disputed, so the evidence supports turnips in living memory, not in prehistory.

# Halloween in Ireland: Living Traditions and the Dates That Matter

Halloween in Ireland is Oíche Shamhna, 31 October, and the Republic builds a week around it: the October bank holiday falls on the last Monday of the month (26 October 2026, 25 October 2027), and schools close for mid-term that same week. Barmbrack with a ring baked in, apples bobbing in a basin and street bonfires are the customs with a paper trail, while fireworks are restricted by law.

Anyone sending Halloween home from abroad should design for a small screen, because 48.3% of views of SubhSandesh's shared pages come from phones, with 90.9% of started pages going on to be published (both platform-wide, neither Halloween-specific). Below: the Irish words, the calendar, six traditions checked against the record, and the two big festivals.

## What is Halloween called in Irish?

Halloween in Irish is Oíche Shamhna, and the [Ó Dónaill dictionary entry for Samhain](https://www.teanglann.ie/en/fgb/samhain) (1977) glosses it plainly as "Hallowe'en". The same entry shows Samhain is also the everyday Irish word for November, so the feast and the month share a name.

Related words, checked on the same site:

- **Oíche Shamhna**: Hallowe'en, the night of 31 October.
- **Lá Samhna**: the first of November, All Hallows.
- **Mí na Samhna**: the month of November.
- **Bairín breac**: barmbrack, literally a speckled loaf.
- **Púca**: a hobgoblin or pooka; "púca na sméar" is the fruit-spoiling pooka the dictionary calls a herald of winter.
- **Bréagriocht**: disguise, which is what a costume is for.

## When is Halloween in Ireland in 2026 and 2027?

Halloween is always 31 October, but the days around it are fixed by statute and by a school circular. The Second Schedule of the Organisation of Working Time Act 1997 lists "the last Monday in October" as a public holiday, and Department of Education [Circular 0018/2026](https://www.into.ie/app/uploads/2026/02/2026.01.30_FINAL_Circular_SSY_2026.29_30_Jan_2026_English.pdf) (30 January 2026, hosted by the INTO) sets the mid-term break with that bank holiday as one of its stated factors.

| Year | Halloween | Bank holiday (Republic) | Schools closed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026 | Saturday 31 October | Monday 26 October | Monday 26 to Friday 30 October |
| 2027 | Sunday 31 October | Monday 25 October | Monday 25 to Friday 29 October |

Both years, the break runs nine days, Saturday to Sunday, with Halloween on its closing weekend. Northern Ireland is part of the UK, and the UK government's bank holiday list for Northern Ireland has no October date in either year.

## 6 Irish Halloween traditions, and whether each one survives

The richest record of how homes kept the night is the Schools' Collection, folklore gathered from more than 50,000 schoolchildren in 1937 to 1939 and now searchable on dúchas.ie. Caitríona Nic Philibín's 2025 study, [Food Traditions in the Folklore of Oíche Shamhna](https://arrow.tudublin.ie/ejfds/vol5/iss1/4), sampled it and found four themes: games, games with divination, the supernatural, and cakes and dishes.

### 1. Barmbrack and the ring

**What it is:** a fruit loaf, bairín breac, cut at teatime on 31 October. **The record:** a pupil in a [Blarney, Co. Cork entry in the Schools' Collection](https://www.duchas.ie/en/cbes/4921724/4893907/5183609) wrote that whoever got the ring would marry within twelve months, and listed four more charms: a pea, a bean, a stick and a rag.

A Boyle, Co. Roscommon pupil gave a ring in a sweet cake the same meaning. **Today:** still the food most tied to the night, but no survey counts how many homes bake or buy one.

### 2. Colcannon and the harvest dishes

**What it is:** mashed potato mixed with cabbage or kale. **The record:** Nic Philibín's abstract lists colcannon with boxty, apple cake and bairín breac among the dishes children named for the feast. **Today:** colcannon is everyday Irish food, so it survives; its tie to 31 October is looser than the brack's.

### 3. Snap apple, or apples in the tub

**What it is:** catching an apple with your mouth, no hands. **The record:** the Blarney pupil called 31 October "snap-apple night" and described a tub half-full of water in the middle of the kitchen after tea, with players getting half-smothered chasing the apple. **Today:** unmeasured, but a basin and a bag of apples make it the easiest old custom to keep.

### 4. The turnip lantern

**What it is:** a hollowed turnip with a face cut in and a candle inside. **The record:** a Bunninadden, Co. Sligo pupil described his father paring a turnip, cutting two eyes and a mouth, and setting it lit on a roadside fence, where, the pupil wrote, it gave one James Byrne a fright; the entry does not name the night. **Today:** we found no count of turnip versus pumpkin carving, and the claim that the jack-o'-lantern is an ancient Irish invention is disputed.

### 5. Bonfires

**What it is:** street and green-space fires lit on the night. **The record:** [Dublin Fire Brigade's Halloween safety page](https://www.dublincity.ie/dublin-fire-brigade/fire-safety-community/fire-safety-halloween) says bonfires are illegal, advises attending organised events only, and reports hundreds of 999 and 112 calls about bonfires over Halloween, especially on the 31st. **Today:** very much alive; the brigade warns that tyres, gas cylinders, aerosols and plastics make the smoke toxic.

### 6. Fireworks

**What it is:** rockets and bangers. **The record:** [section 68 of the Criminal Justice Act 2006](https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2006/act/26/section/68/enacted/en/html) rewrote section 80 of the Explosives Act 1875: igniting a firework, or throwing a lit one at a person or property, is an offence, as is holding fireworks to sell without an import licence. On indictment the maximum is a €10,000 fine or five years in prison; for lighting and selling, low-hazard fireworks other than bangers fall outside the definition.

**Today:** the fire brigade still calls Halloween known for bonfires and fireworks. This summarises the section as enacted in 2006, not legal advice.

## Irish Halloween traditions compared: what, where and how alive

Each row rates a tradition on the evidence it actually has. "Unmeasured" means no survey exists, not that the custom has died.

| Tradition | What it is | Where and when recorded | Still common today? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Barmbrack and charms | Fruit loaf with ring, pea, bean, stick and rag | Blarney, Co. Cork, 1937 to 1939 | Yes as a food; the charm set is unmeasured |
| Colcannon, boxty, apple cake | Harvest dishes for the feast | Schools' Collection sample, analysed 2025 | Yes as food; Halloween link varies |
| Snap apple and divination games | Apples in a tub; saucers of water, clay and a ring | Blarney and Boyle, 1937 to 1939 | Apple game yes; saucer divination called extinct in the 1930s |
| Turnip lantern | Carved turnip with a candle | Bunninadden, Co. Sligo, 1937 to 1939 | Not measured |
| Bonfires and fireworks | Street fires; rockets and bangers | Dublin Fire Brigade; 2006 Act | Bonfires yes, though illegal; fireworks restricted |

The food and the fire have lasted, while the fortune-telling games were fading even when children wrote them down nearly ninety years ago. That fits Nic Philibín's reading, which puts food at the centre of the night.

## Where can you spend Halloween in Ireland? Púca and Derry

The two best-known festivals sit in different jurisdictions. The Púca Festival, named for the shape-shifting spirit, runs 29 October to 1 November 2026 across Trim and Athboy in Co. Meath, with fire performances, music and folklore, and its own site marks the programme "subject to licence". Trim is in the Republic, so the bank holiday and mid-term apply and you pay in euro.

Derry Halloween, which bills itself as Europe's largest Halloween festival, runs 28 October to 1 November 2026 for its 40th anniversary, with a homegrown parade and fireworks on 31 October and the Awakening the Walled City Trail on three nights along the 400-year-old walls. Derry is in Northern Ireland: sterling, no October bank holiday, and separate fireworks rules. Neither festival had announced 2027 dates in October 2026, so check each official site before booking.

## How much of Irish Halloween is still a living tradition?

Less than tourism copy suggests. The dúchas.ie topic index holds about 934 Schools' Collection items tagged Halloween, and the decline shows even there: the Boyle pupil described a blindfold game with three saucers, of water, clay and a ring, then added it was "never practised nowadays".

What survives needs no belief: a loaf, a tub of apples, a fire, a week off school. Food-specific studies of the feast are few, Nic Philibín notes, and no national survey counts how many households still bake a brack, so any percentage for that is a guess.

## Sending Halloween to family in Ireland from abroad

For the diaspora, the gap is distance: brack cannot be posted across an ocean in time for the 31st. The [interactive Halloween card](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) carries the night to one person instead. Fill in both names, write a letter, add six photos at most, choose a word for the pumpkin; your relative then raps three times at a small haunted house, carves the lantern until that word lights up, finds your letter with a torch in a dark attic and mixes a potion out of three to five shared memories.

Pick the family setting and the last question turns into "Will you be my favourite little pumpkin?"; the Kids tone brings round, blushing ghosts with no gore or jump scares. You hear by email the moment their first answer lands, and nobody on the receiving end installs anything or signs up. Platform-wide, each page averages 11.1 views, a hint that links get reopened, though the figure cannot say by whom.

Where a voice matters more than text, the [premium Halloween page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) holds a voice note of at most 60 seconds, a dozen photos, plus an unlock time keeping it sealed until 31 October. Its listing estimates ten minutes to build, against five.

### When the link is the wrong gift for an Irish household

At the same table on the night, hand over the brack and forget the link. Its interface is English-only, and its lantern is a pumpkin. It is built for a single recipient, not a houseful of guests, and a relative who never taps links on a phone deserves a call instead.

Brief said to cite gov.ie for fireworks and school dates; gov.ie is unreachable, so the Irish Statute Book and the Department circular PDF hosted by INTO (the primary teachers' union) are used instead.

Neither lists 2027 dates.

Boyle, Co. Roscommon (duchas.ie/en/cbes/4758456/4745663/4778269 and continuation page) and Bunninadden, Co. Sligo (duchas.ie/en/cbes/4701755/4699729/4714689) Schools' Collection entries were read and are described by place but not linked.
